label: Density Estimation on Special Manifolds
notes: We open the chapter by asking how to estimate an unknown density when the data live on a curved space such as the Stiefel or Grassmann manifold. The kernel estimator generalizes the Euclidean picture by replacing line bumps with rotationally symmetric bumps placed at each observed frame.

label: Data on Special Manifolds
notes: The Stiefel manifold collects orthonormal frames while the Grassmann manifold collects subspaces. Both inherit rotation invariance from the orthogonal group, and that invariance is exactly the symmetry our kernels should respect so that estimates do not privilege any direction.

label: The Manifold Kernel Estimator
notes: A manifold kernel estimator averages a kernel evaluated between each sample and the query point, then divides by a normalizing constant so the result integrates to one. The kernel depends only on an invariant alignment between frames, which keeps the estimator equivariant under the group action.

label: Rotationally Symmetric Kernels
notes: We focus on rotationally symmetric kernels whose value depends only on the trace of the aligned product. The matrix Langevin form supplies a natural template: it concentrates mass near a center and decays smoothly, mirroring the Gaussian bump used in the flat case.

label: Concentration as Inverse Bandwidth
notes: The concentration parameter plays the role of an inverse bandwidth. A large concentration produces a narrow spike that resolves fine structure, while a small concentration produces a broad bump that smooths aggressively. Choosing it well is the central tuning problem of the chapter.

label: Bumps Summing to a Density
notes: Here we see the estimator built constructively. Each sample contributes one rotationally symmetric bump on the circle, and the normalized sum of these bumps yields a smooth estimated density. Regions with many nearby samples accumulate overlapping bumps and rise into peaks.

label: Bias of the Estimator
notes: Bias arises because smoothing pulls the estimate toward a local average of the true density. Expanding in the bandwidth shows the leading bias scales with curvature of the density and with the inverse concentration, so heavy smoothing systematically flattens peaks and fills valleys.

label: Variance of the Estimator
notes: Variance measures the estimator's sensitivity to the particular sample drawn. Concentrated kernels use fewer effective neighbors, so the variance grows with concentration and shrinks with sample size. The variance term and the bias term pull the bandwidth in opposite directions.

label: The Bias-Variance Tradeoff
notes: The mean integrated squared error sums squared bias and variance. Undersmoothing yields a jagged spiky estimate dominated by variance, while oversmoothing yields a washed out estimate dominated by bias. The optimal concentration balances the two competing error sources.

label: Bandwidth Selection
notes: Because the optimal concentration depends on unknown smoothness, we choose it from data. Cross validation scores candidate concentrations by held out likelihood, while plug in rules estimate the curvature term directly. Both target the concentration that minimizes the integrated error.

label: Consistency
notes: Consistency requires the bandwidth to shrink while the effective sample count grows. If concentration increases and the sample size times the kernel volume diverges, both bias and variance vanish, so the estimator converges to the true density in mean square as samples accumulate.

label: Recap and Outlook
notes: We recap the chapter: rotationally symmetric kernels, concentration as inverse bandwidth, the bias variance tradeoff, data driven bandwidth selection, and consistency. These tools transfer directly to clustering, mode hunting, and goodness of fit testing on Stiefel and Grassmann manifolds.
